With a nerve complaint at the elbow, first ask whether it is weakness, pain or both, and whether the numbness is a true loss of sensation. Then find the site: the commonest is the ulnar nerve behind the medial epicondyle.
1. Weakness and abnormal sensation around the elbow

• Weakness is a very common complaint when there is pain
    • first question: is it weakness, pain, or both? · pain without weakness is common · pain with weakness is common · weakness without pain is uncommon, which narrows the list
    • second question: if the weakness is real, what is causing it?
  • Abnormal sensation
    • a nerve injury can give too much feeling (tingling, spontaneous pain) and too little (numbness) at the same time
    • tingling or pain can come from nerve, muscle, tendon, ligament, bone or joint, or be referred from elsewhere
    • true sensory loss is neurogenic: it comes from the peripheral or central nervous system
2. Ulnar neuropathy at the elbow (cubital tunnel syndrome)

• What it is: the ulnar nerve squeezed or irritated where it runs behind the medial epicondyle
  • Causes
    • direct trauma (hitting the "funny bone") · repeated pressure (leaning on a desk)
    • long periods with the elbow bent stretch the nerve (during sleep)
    • the nerve slipping over the epicondyle as the elbow bends · thickened ligament · medial epicondylosis
  • Presents as
    • medial elbow pain
    • numbness and tingling in the ring and little fingers ("they fall asleep")
    • weakness of the hand, because the ulnar nerve drives the interossei · lower motor neuron weakness only in muscles the ulnar nerve supplies below the elbow
    • medial forearm skin: spared in the medwiki note, because a branch of the medial cord supplies it (sources differ: upper-year notes describe numbness running from the medial forearm into the ring and little fingers - check the slides)
  • Exam: Tinel sign positive at the elbow (tapping over the nerve sends tingling down its territory) · map sensory loss · test the hand muscles · the nerve may slip on bending
  • Investigations
    • electromyography (EMG) or a nerve conduction study separates irritation from real nerve damage · needed sooner if weakness is significant or getting worse
    • nerve ultrasound or MRI · X-ray if elbow arthritis or an old injury is suspected (upper-year notes)
  • Treatment
    • education matters most: irritation (neuritis) is fully reversible, and so is mild nerve damage, because peripheral nerves regrow
    • avoid pressure on the elbow (pad it, change the workstation)
    • avoid bending the elbow fully at night: a towel splint or elbow pad
    • medication is neither needed nor helpful
    • surgery for severe or progressive cases: ulnar neurolysis (freeing it from scar) or transposition (moving it out from behind the epicondyle)

The thumb's CMC joint is a saddle, which is what lets the thumb oppose. Thenar muscles = recurrent branch of the median nerve; nearly every other intrinsic muscle = deep branch of the ulnar. PAD and DAB: palmar interossei adduct, dorsal interossei abduct. Superficial arch = mostly ulnar; deep arch = mostly radial.

blocks.html: 2. Fascia of the wrist and hand

• Palmar aponeurosis: where palmaris longus inserts · longitudinal fibres fan from the flexor retinaculum to the four fingers and blend with their tendon sheaths · its septa divide the palm into compartments
    • upper-year notes: in Dupuytren's contracture it thickens and scars, pulling fingers into fixed flexion; the diseased tissue has to be cut out
  • Palmar carpal ligament: a thickening of the forearm fascia, continuous with the extensor retinaculum on the back · superficial and proximal to the flexor retinaculum
  • Flexor retinaculum: deeper · the roof of the carpal tunnel · spans scaphoid and trapezium (lateral) to pisiform and hook of the hamate (medial)
  • Carpal tunnel: carpal bones for a floor, flexor retinaculum for a roof
    • inside: 4 flexor digitorum superficialis tendons · 4 flexor digitorum profundus tendons · flexor pollicis longus · the median nerve
    • outside, on top of the retinaculum: the ulnar nerve and artery · the palmar cutaneous branch of the median nerve · palmaris longus tendon
  • Fibrous digital sheaths (flexor pulleys): tunnels of fibrous tissue binding the flexor tendons to each finger's bones · work as pulleys and stop the tendons bowstringing
  • Synovial sheaths: fluid-filled sleeves inside the fibrous sheaths that let the tendons glide
    • upper-year notes: an infected sheath (tenosynovitis) gives a swollen finger that hurts to move; usually it stays in that finger but can spread into the palm and forearm

lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Snuffbox tenderness after a FOOSH with a normal X-ray is treated as a scaphoid fracture anyway: blood reaches the scaphoid from its far end, so a missed fracture can end in non-union or osteonecrosis. Distal radius X-ray = short (ulnar variance), crooked (volar tilt), smooth (step over 1 mm needs fixing). Make the deformity worse to unlock it, then reduce and cast with a 3-point mould. Treatment is forgiving at the extremes of age; middle-aged, active patients need the most. Tingling in the thumb and first two fingers after a wrist fracture = acute carpal tunnel syndrome.

Two fractures from a fall on an outstretched hand (FOOSH): the distal radius, judged on X-ray by three questions (is it short? crooked? smooth?), and the scaphoid, which can hide on the first X-ray and lose its blood supply if missed.
1. Distal radius fracture

• What it is: a very common break of the end of the radius, usually from a FOOSH
    • upper-year notes: a Colles fracture (a complete break in the last 2 cm of the radius) is the most common forearm fracture
    • often comes with a torn ligament or a scaphoid fracture · if the anatomy is not restored, the wrist works poorly

Volar tilt on the side (lateral) view

Closer to 0°, or tilted toward the back

• The medwiki note words positive variance as the ulna projecting further, then adds "radius longer than the ulna" in brackets, which contradicts itself (sources differ: the condition note and upper-year notes both tie positive variance to a shortened radius - check the slides)
  • Treatment depends on age
    • forgiving at the extremes: a young bone remodels itself straight · an older patient puts less load on the wrist and has laxer ligaments, so fewer symptoms
    • middle-aged or active patients need more intensive treatment
  • Closed reduction and casting
    • ① analgesia is essential: hematoma block (1% lidocaine into the fracture) · regional nerve block · conscious sedation
    • ② sustained pull along the bone (by hand or finger traps) relaxes the muscles
    • ③ manipulate: often make the deformity worse first to unlock the fragments, then correct it
    • ④ cast: cotton padding under plaster (cheap, mouldable, heavy) or fibreglass (can be waterproof, clearer on X-ray) · 3-point mould
    • ⑤ X-ray to confirm the alignment
  • Surgery if closed reduction fails: external fixation (pins through the skin held by rods, for a few weeks) · open reduction with plates and screws
  • Upper-year case: a displaced fracture plus tingling in the thumb, index and middle fingers = acute carpal tunnel syndrome from the fragment pressing on the median nerve → open reduction, fixation and carpal tunnel release

blocks.html: 2. Scaphoid fracture

• What it is: the scaphoid is the most commonly fractured carpal bone · younger patients · FOOSH
    • many shrug it off as a sprain and it heals, but it is hard to diagnose, and a late diagnosis brings complications
  • Why it goes wrong: its blood enters at the far (distal) end and flows back toward the near end · a break through the middle cuts the proximal part off
  • Presents as: swelling and tenderness in the anatomical snuffbox · wrist pain · thumb pain, especially on the push-pull test of the thumb
  • Investigations
    • X-ray is usually enough, but can look normal
    • high suspicion with a normal X-ray: treat it as fractured, then repeat the X-ray in a couple of weeks (the fracture line shows as the bone heals) or go to CT, MRI or a bone scan
  • Treatment
    • cast: undisplaced fractures and distal-pole fractures · until healed, about 8 weeks (upper-year notes)
    • surgery (a screw): displaced fractures and proximal-pole fractures
  • Complications: non-union (does not heal) · osteonecrosis (bone death) · late arthritis, which may need a wrist fusion that costs flexion and extension

lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Median nerve = LOAF (lateral 2 lumbricals, opponens pollicis, abductor and flexor pollicis brevis) and the palm side of the lateral 3½ fingers; the deep ulnar branch runs every other intrinsic muscle. blocks.html: 2. Carpal tunnel syndrome

• Definition: the median nerve compressed inside the carpal tunnel · the most common nerve injury of all
    • usually swollen, inflamed synovial sheaths round the flexor tendons squeezing the most sensitive structure in the tunnel, the nerve
  • Causes - anything that shrinks the space or makes the nerve more vulnerable
    • less space: fracture · flexor tenosynovitis · overuse · ganglion cyst · inflammation (rheumatologic disease) · pregnancy (edema) · acromegaly
    • more vulnerable nerve: diabetes · amyloidosis · alcohol
  • Presents as
    • numbness and tingling in the thumb, index, middle and half the ring finger · hand and wrist pain
    • worse at night (sleeping with bent wrists) and with sustained wrist flexion or extension (driving, holding a phone)
    • thumb weakness from the LOAF muscles (abductor pollicis brevis) · thenar wasting if advanced
    • the central palm is spared (its palmar cutaneous branch leaves before the tunnel) · forearm muscles are normal
  • Exam: Phalen's sign (more sensitive) · Tinel sign at the wrist
  • Differential: C6 radiculopathy (numb lateral forearm and thumb, but weak wrist extensors rather than LOAF) · tendinopathy of the thumb tendons · trapeziometacarpal osteoarthritis (thumb-base arthritis) · de Quervain syndrome
  • Investigations: electromyography / nerve conduction study - separates it from C6 radiculopathy and from muscle or bone problems, and grades severity
  • Treatment
    • education: very common · reversible if caught early · hand position
    • conservative: rigid wrist brace at night only · avoid aggravating positions and vibrating tools · steroid injection into the tunnel
    • surgery: carpal tunnel release (cut the flexor retinaculum) - very effective
  • Acute version: a displaced distal radius fracture pressing on the nerve (Part 1)

blocks.html: 3. Guyon's canal syndrome (ulnar canal syndrome)

• Definition: the ulnar nerve compressed in Guyon's canal (pisiform, hook of hamate, pisohamate ligament) at the wrist
    • less common than ulnar compression at the elbow (cubital tunnel syndrome)
  • Cause: almost always outside pressure - ⚠ "handlebar neuropathy" in cyclists, from pressure over the hook of the hamate with the wrists extended · also fracture, ganglion cyst, inflammation · intrinsic causes are rare
  • Presents as: numbness and tingling in the little finger and half the ring finger · weak intrinsic hand muscles · wasting if long-standing · clawing of fingers 4-5 can occur, but finger flexion is kept and the hand is not pulled toward the thumb (unlike an elbow lesion)
  • Differential: C8 radiculopathy · cubital tunnel syndrome · tendinopathy
  • Investigations: EMG / nerve conduction study, as for carpal tunnel
  • Treatment: education (hand position, handlebar pressure; reversible early) · padded gloves, different handlebars · Guyon's canal release if needed

Osteoarthritis = joint space lost, osteophytes, subchondral sclerosis and cysts, at any joint. Distal radius displacement and angulation are read on the lateral view. Scaphoid fracture hides: get the scaphoid series (ulnar deviation) and, if needed, MRI.

One rule runs through the lecture: one view is never enough. Each joint has a standard set of plain X-ray views, and each common injury hides on one of them - the direction of a shoulder dislocation, the tilt of a distal radius fracture, a scaphoid fracture line.

cols: What the extra view is for
rows: Dislocation: humeral head off the glenoid · over 90% anterior, but confirm on the Y-view
AP of the hand and wrist · lateral of the wrist
Lateral shows tilt and displacement · the scaphoid series adds views to find a scaphoid fracture

blocks.html: 1. Shoulder

• Views
    • AP: acromion, clavicle, coracoid, glenoid, humeral head, greater and lesser tuberosities
    • Axillary: beam through the armpit (axilla) · shows the glenohumeral and acromioclavicular joints
    • Y-view (trans-scapular): the scapula seen side-on as a "Y" (acromion, coracoid, scapular body) · separates anterior from posterior
  • Shoulder dislocation: humeral head no longer lined up with the glenoid fossa
    • direction needs more than one view · over 90% are anterior, but only the Y-view proves it
  • Osteoarthritis: the four signs (section 4)

blocks.alt: x-ray - normal vs. non-inflammatory shoulder arthritis.png
blocks.cap: Normal shoulder vs shoulder osteoarthritis: joint space lost, osteophytes on the humeral head, sclerosis

blocks.html: 2. Elbow

• Views: AP (medial and lateral epicondyles, olecranon, trochlea, capitellum, radial head and neck) · lateral (radial head, coronoid, olecranon, the fossae)
  • Osteoarthritis: the same four signs
3. Wrist and hand

• Views
    • AP of the hand: phalanges, metacarpals, carpals; the MCP, PIP, DIP and CMC joints
    • AP of the wrist: the eight carpal bones over the radius and ulna
    • Lateral of the wrist: radius, lunate, scaphoid and 3rd metacarpal seen side-on
  • Scaphoid series: several projections (PA, oblique, lateral, PA with ulnar deviation) for a suspected scaphoid fracture
    • ulnar deviation lifts the scaphoid off the radius for a clearer look
    • the fracture is easy to miss on X-ray · MRI shows it better, though a careful look often finds it
  • Distal radius fracture: read both the AP and the lateral
    • transverse = the line runs straight across
    • dorsal displacement = the distal piece shifted toward the back of the hand (lateral view)
    • angulation = described as anterior or posterior (lateral view)
    • upper-year notes add the three checks from Part 1: too short? too crooked? joint surface smooth?

blocks.cap: Lateral wrist X-ray with the radius, lunate, scaphoid and 3rd metacarpal outlined

blocks.html: 4. Osteoarthritis on any X-ray

• Loss of joint space
  • Osteophytes - bone spurs
  • Subchondral sclerosis - extra-white (dense) bone under the joint
  • Subchondral cysts - dark (lucent) holes under the joint

lectures.name: Anatomy of the Hip Joint
lectures.title: Anatomy of the hip joint
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ The medial circumflex femoral artery carries most of the femoral head's blood along the neck, so a femoral neck fracture risks avascular necrosis. Hip = stability over mobility; shoulder = mobility over stability. The iliofemoral (Y) ligament is the strongest in the body, and the capsule screws the head in on extension. The labrum deepens the socket; the ligament of the head adds no strength. Iliac crest = L4; ischial tuberosity = sitting bone and hamstring origin; ASIS felt, AIIS not.

The hip is the shoulder's opposite: it gives up some movement to be the most stable joint in the body. The lecture builds it from the bones (pelvis, femur, and the tibia and fibula below), then the capsule and ligaments that hold it, then the arteries whose failure explains why a femoral neck fracture is so dangerous.
1. The pelvis (hip bone)
• Three bones - ilium, ischium, pubis - which all meet in the acetabulum, the socket for the femoral head

rows: Top of the crest = L4 level (lumbar puncture landmark) · back part is the origin of gluteus maximus
Felt at the front of the hip · origin of sartorius and tensor fasciae latae
Cannot be felt · attachment for muscles (rectus femoris) and ligaments
The "dimple of Venus" on the lower back
Top edge of the greater sciatic notch
Divides the greater sciatic notch (above) from the lesser (below) · sacrospinous ligament attaches
Takes your weight when sitting · origin of the hamstrings
Front bony point · inguinal ligament attaches (the medwiki note links it to the pubic symphysis)
Passage from pelvis to thigh for the obturator nerve and vessels

blocks.cap: The hip bone from the side and from inside: ilium (purple), pubis (orange) and ischium (green) meeting at the acetabulum, with the iliac spines, sciatic notches, ischial tuberosity and obturator foramen

blocks.html: 2. Femur, tibia and fibula

• Femur: the longest, thickest bone, and the only bone of the thigh
    • head (into the acetabulum) · neck (head to shaft) · greater trochanter (lateral, felt through the skin) · lesser trochanter (medial and posterior - tells you which way the femur faces) · intertrochanteric line (front) and crest (back) · linea aspera (back of the shaft) · medial and lateral condyles (knee)
  • Tibia: the big, weight-bearing bone of the leg · condyles form the tibial plateau · tibial tuberosity = where the patellar ligament inserts
  • Fibula: always lateral to the tibia (tells left from right) · its head is not part of the knee joint · no weight-bearing role
3. The hip joint: built for stability

• Type: ball-and-socket synovial joint, moves in every axis
  • Stable because of
    • bony fit - more than half the femoral head sits in the acetabulum
    • strong ligaments - including the strongest in the body
    • muscles around it (dynamic support)
• Versus the shoulder: the hip gives up some mobility for stability; the glenohumeral joint gives up stability for mobility

rows: Attaches to the intertrochanteric line in front, but not to the back of the femur · its fibres twist tight in extension, "screwing" the head into the socket, so standing costs the muscles little · also stops over-abduction
Strongest ligament in the body · front and top · limits extension
Fibrocartilage ring on the acetabular rim that deepens the socket · the transverse acetabular ligament bridges its gap at the bottom
Ligament of the head of the femur
Runs from the head into the acetabulum (the one part of the head not covered by synovium) · adds no real strength · carries a small artery

blocks.cap: The hip's capsular ligaments from the front (iliofemoral, pubofemoral) and from behind (ischiofemoral), with the zona orbicularis round the femoral neck

blocks.html: 4. Blood supply of the femoral head

rows: Largest branch of the femoral artery
Main artery of the hip region · gives the two circumflex arteries
The biggest supply to the head and neck (via retinacular arteries along the neck)
Wraps round the neck with the medial one
Artery of the ligament of the head

Runs inside the ligament · minor in adults (sources differ: the medwiki note says it is the only supply to the head in children whose growth plates have not fused; upper-year notes call it minor and often inadequate - check the slides)

blocks.html:
• Collateral circulation: the inferior gluteal artery joins the circumflex arteries, so the hip (and leg) still get blood if the proximal femoral artery is blocked
  • Why it matters: a femoral neck fracture tears the circumflex vessels → the head is left on the small ligament artery → avascular necrosis (see the clinical lecture)

blocks.cap: Arteries of the femoral head: the deep femoral artery giving the medial and lateral circumflex arteries round the neck, and the artery of the ligament of the head

lectures.name: Clinical Approach to the Hip Joint
lectures.title: Clinical approach to the hip joint
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Hip fracture = an older person after a fall with groin pain and a short, externally rotated, abducted leg; suspect it even when the pain is mild, X-ray first and CT if the X-ray is clear. A displaced femoral neck fracture needs urgent arthroplasty because the circumflex blood supply is torn. Always ask why they fell: ECG, troponin, electrolytes, chest X-ray. Afterwards: early mobilisation, heparin for clots, fall prevention and bone health. Posterior dislocation rotates the leg in; a fracture rotates it out.

The medwiki note for this lecture is one condition: the hip fracture. An older person falls, has groin pain and a short, externally rotated leg - confirm the fracture, then ask why they fell, operate within 1-2 days, and prevent the complications that kill a quarter of them within a year. The other hip problems (osteoarthritis, tendinopathy and bursitis, sacroiliac joint) are covered in 05 - Clinical Approach to Hip Pain.
1. Examining any hip (upper-year notes)

• Look: body habitus · swelling, redness, asymmetry or wasting, deformity, scars · alignment (fixed flexion from the side, an externally rotated leg) · gait (antalgic = limping from pain · Trendelenburg: weak hip abductors let the pelvis drop on the other side)
  • Feel: bony points (ASIS, front of the joint, pubic symphysis) · muscles (quadriceps, tensor fasciae latae, iliotibial band, glutes, piriformis, hamstrings)
  • Move: active and passive range · FABER (flexion, abduction, external rotation) · FADIR (flexion, adduction, internal rotation)
  • Investigations: X-ray first (fracture, arthritis, tumour, avascular necrosis) · ultrasound (bursitis, tendons, guiding injections) · CT if a fracture is suspected but not seen · MRI (soft tissue, stress fractures)
  • Treatment, in general: education and expectations · RICE (rest, ice, compression, elevation), weight management, exercise · topical or oral pain relief · steroid injections · surgery
2. Hip fracture: who and why

• Definition: a hip fracture is a fracture of the proximal femur, usually the femoral neck (rarely the head) · an intertrochanteric fracture lies outside the capsule
  • Who: mostly older people after a simple fall (9 in 10) · young people only after high-energy trauma (car crashes)
    • women 2:1 (upper-year notes: lifetime risk 18% vs 6%) · but men are more likely to die afterwards
    • 20-30% die within a year · half never return to independent living
  • Risk factors: almost always a fall on top of weak bone

rows: Previous falls · weakness (stroke, peripheral vascular disease, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease) · polypharmacy: sedatives, diuretics, psychotropics, antiarrhythmics · poor nutrition · poor eyesight

Previous fragility fracture or vertebral compression fracture · long-term steroids · early menopause or hypogonadism · malabsorption · hyperparathyroidism · osteopenia · parental hip fracture · alcohol · smoking · low body weight · rheumatoid arthritis · age 65+

blocks.html: • Upper-year notes add: hyperthyroidism and inflammatory bowel disease · low socioeconomic status · levothyroxine, loop diuretics, proton-pump inhibitors
3. Hip fracture: presentation and workup

• Presents as (SOCRATES): groin pain, or lateral upper-thigh pain in an intertrochanteric fracture · sudden, after a fall · sharp or deep ache · may radiate to the knee · worse with movement and weight-bearing, eased by keeping still
    • ⚠ severity varies hugely - pain can be minimal when still, so suspect it in any older person who falls, however small the fall
  • Exam
    • look: leg shortened, externally rotated, abducted · cannot bear weight
    • feel: tender over the hip
    • move: painful range, especially log roll and straight leg raise (upper-year notes add axial loading)
    • check pulses, sensation and movement below - especially the sciatic nerve (ankle up and down)

Types of hip fracture along the proximal femur: subcapital and transcervical neck fractures, intertrochanteric, subtrochanteric, and greater or lesser trochanter fractures

blocks.html: 4. Hip fracture: treatment and after

• Surgery for almost everyone - gets them weight-bearing sooner and avoids the harm of lying still
    • displaced femoral neck → urgent, and almost always an arthroplasty: hemiarthroplasty (femoral head only) or total hip (head and socket) · screws are rarely enough
    • intertrochanteric and subtrochanteric → surgery too
    • why the neck is urgent: the fracture tears the circumflex arteries that feed the head → avascular necrosis (see 03.1 - Anatomy of the Hip Joint)
  • After surgery
    • early mobilisation · physiotherapy
    • low-molecular-weight heparin for 14-30 days against clots (upper-year notes: 30 days)
    • fall prevention: optimise other illnesses, stop risky drugs, gait aids, occupational therapy home check
    • bone health: treat osteoporosis, vitamin D and calcium · consider antiresorptives (bisphosphonates)
  • Complications: venous thromboembolism · pneumonia (a common cause of death) · muscle wasting · wound infection, urinary infection · delirium and mental decline · pressure sores · non-union
5. Other hip-joint injuries in the anatomy (upper-year notes)

• Posterior hip dislocation: a car crash driving force along the femur · leg shortened and medially (internally) rotated · ⚠ the sciatic nerve can be stretched or crushed
  • Congenital dislocation: a malformed acetabulum or femur gives a poor fit and an unstable joint

lectures.name: Anatomy of the Gluteal Region & Thigh
lectures.title: Anatomy of the gluteal region and thigh
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Piriformis is the landmark: only the superior gluteal nerve and vessels leave above it; the sciatic, inferior gluteal and pudendal nerves leave below, and the superior gluteal nerve is the one behind a Trendelenburg sign. A weak right gluteus medius drops the LEFT side of the pelvis. Front = femoral, inner = obturator, back = sciatic - except the hamstring part of adductor magnus (tibial) and the short head of biceps (common fibular). NAVEL from outer to inner; the femoral nerve sits outside the sheath. Injections go upper outer quadrant, away from the sciatic nerve.

Two organising ideas carry the whole lecture. In the buttock, piriformis is the landmark: only the superior gluteal vessels and nerve leave the pelvis above it, everything else below. In the thigh, three compartments each have one job and one nerve - front: femoral, inside: obturator, back: sciatic.
1. Passageways out of the pelvis
• The sacrotuberous and sacrospinous ligaments turn the sciatic notches into two foramina

rows: Inferior gluteal vessels and nerve · sciatic nerve · posterior cutaneous nerve of the thigh · nerve to quadratus femoris · pudendal nerve, internal pudendal vessels, nerve to obturator internus
Pudendal nerve, internal pudendal vessels, nerve to obturator internus - the same ones, hooking back in to reach the perineum

blocks.html: 2. Muscles of the buttock

rows: Main hip extensor · standing up from sitting
Abduct and medially rotate the hip · hold the pelvis level when walking
Keeps the iliotibial band tight · helps flex the hip
Lateral rotators: piriformis · obturator internus · superior and inferior gemellus · quadratus femoris
Their own small nerves (nerve to piriformis, to obturator internus, to quadratus femoris)
Laterally rotate the thigh · steady the femoral head in the socket - the hip's "rotator cuff"

blocks.html:
• Trendelenburg sign: gluteus medius and minimus contract on the standing leg to stop the pelvis tipping toward the swinging one
    • weak (muscle damage, or the superior gluteal nerve injured, e.g. in hip replacement) → the pelvis drops on the opposite, unsupported side
    • to compensate, the patient leans away from the dropping side to let the swinging foot clear the ground
  • Intramuscular injections go in the upper outer quadrant of the buttock, away from the sciatic nerve

blocks.cap: Nerves of the buttock: the superior gluteal nerve leaving above piriformis; the inferior gluteal, sciatic, posterior cutaneous nerve of the thigh and pudendal nerves leaving below it

blocks.html: 3. The thigh's three compartments

rows: Iliopsoas · sartorius · quadriceps (rectus femoris, vastus lateralis, medialis, intermedius) · pectineus
Adductor longus, brevis, magnus · gracilis · obturator externus

blocks.html:
• Exceptions to "one nerve per compartment"
    • adductor magnus has two parts: adductor part (obturator) + hamstring part (tibial division of the sciatic)
    • short head of biceps femoris = common fibular division of the sciatic · all other hamstrings = tibial division
    • pectineus = femoral nerve (upper-year notes)
  • Quadriceps: the only knee extensors · one tendon to the tibial tuberosity, with the patella inside it for leverage · rectus femoris is the only one that crosses the hip, so it also helps flex it
  • Pes anserinus ("goose's foot"): sartorius + gracilis + semitendinosus insert together on the inner upper tibia
  • Injuries
    • hamstring strain: active contraction against a passive stretch · bad pain and bruising · forced hip flexion with a straight knee can pull off the ischial tuberosity
    • groin pull: the adductors, same mechanism · big bruise · RICE (rest, ice, compression, elevation) and anti-inflammatories
    • teenagers: the growth plate is weaker than the tendon → a hard hip flexion can pull off the ASIS (anterior superior iliac spine)
4. Popliteal fossa

• Diamond behind the knee: biceps femoris (upper outer) · semimembranosus and semitendinosus (upper inner) · the two heads of gastrocnemius (below)
  • Contents: tibial and common fibular nerves (the sciatic usually splits at the top of the diamond) · popliteal artery and vein · end of the small saphenous vein · popliteal lymph nodes · fat
    • from deep to superficial: artery → vein → nerve
  • Popliteal aneurysm: the most common aneurysm outside the trunk · 80% have no symptoms · half are on both sides · risk of clot, embolism and rupture → high-risk ones are operated on · think of it with a pulsatile lump behind the knee

blocks.cap: Popliteal fossa: bounded by biceps femoris, semimembranosus, semitendinosus and the gastrocnemius heads, holding the tibial and common fibular nerves and the popliteal artery and vein

blocks.html: 5. Arteries and veins

rows: Gluteus medius and minimus · leaves above piriformis
Joins the circumflex arteries round the hip (collateral flow)
External iliac, under the inguinal ligament
Front and inner thigh · becomes the popliteal after the adductor hiatus
Superficial in the femoral triangle, so easily injured
Perforating branches pierce adductor magnus to the back of the thigh · medial and lateral circumflex to the femoral head
The circumflex, inferior gluteal and 1st perforating arteries link up, so the leg survives if the femoral artery is tied off
Longest vein; superficial, up the inner leg and thigh → through the saphenous opening of the fascia lata into the femoral vein
Harvested for coronary bypass grafts (sources differ on what is at risk: the medwiki note says the femoral artery, upper-year notes the saphenous nerve beside it - check the slides)
Deep vein of the thigh → external iliac vein

blocks.html: 6. Nerves of the thigh

rows: Gluteus medius, minimus, tensor fasciae latae
Below piriformis, down the back of the thigh
Largest nerve in the body = tibial + common fibular nerves in one sheath · hamstrings
Posterior cutaneous nerve of the thigh
Skin of the lower buttock and back of the thigh
Out the greater foramen, straight back in through the lesser
Under the inguinal ligament, lateral to the vessels
Front-of-thigh muscles and skin (sources differ: the medwiki note says skin of the inner thigh - check the slides) · knee-jerk reflex tests it (L3-L4)
Skin of the inner knee, leg and foot
Lateral cutaneous nerve of the thigh
Under the inguinal ligament beside the ASIS
Adductors (not the hamstring part of magnus) · some inner-thigh skin

blocks.html: • Sciatic nerve injury ("sciatica"): pain, tingling or numbness from buttock to foot · one cause is piriformis syndrome, where the nerve runs through piriformis and is squeezed
7. Lymph nodes

• Superficial inguinal: thigh · inner leg · perineum and external genitalia · abdominal wall below the umbilicus
  • Deep inguinal: inside the femoral sheath, beside the femoral vein
  • Both → external iliac nodes
8. Femoral triangle

• Borders: inguinal ligament (top) · sartorius (outer side) · adductor longus (inner side)
  • Contents, outer to inner - "NAVEL": Nerve (femoral) · Artery · Vein · Empty space (femoral canal) · Lymph nodes (deep inguinal)
    • the femoral sheath wraps the artery, vein and canal - not the nerve · its entrance is the femoral ring
    • a loop of bowel through the femoral ring = femoral hernia (upper-year notes)
  • Adductor canal (sartorius, vastus medialis, adductor longus) carries the femoral vessels down to the adductor hiatus, where they pass behind the knee and become the popliteal vessels

lectures.name: Clinical Approach to Hip Pain
lectures.title: Clinical approach to hip pain
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Point first: groin = inside the joint, lateral = greater trochanter, buttock = deep gluteal, sacroiliac or spine. Can't put socks on → hip arthritis; tender trochanter but socks fine → GTPS. Internal rotation is the first movement lost in hip osteoarthritis. Clicking and locking in a young active woman → labral tear, usually from FAI. Burning lateral thigh with no weakness → meralgia paresthetica. Buttock pain worse sitting, with sciatica → piriformis; MRI the spine first.

blocks.html: Built from upper-year notes and the medwiki note. Not yet checked against this year's lecture slides.

First ask where the patient means by "hip". True hip pain is anterior hip or groin pain and usually comes from inside the joint; lateral pain points to the greater trochanter, and posterior (buttock) pain to the deep gluteal space, the sacroiliac joint or the spine. Hip fracture is covered in 03.2 - Clinical Approach to the Hip Joint.
1. Locate the pain, then work it up

osteoarthritis · femoroacetabular impingement

fracture · septic arthritis"] B -->|"Lateral hip"| D["Greater trochanteric pain syndrome
(gluteal tendinopathy ± trochanteric bursitis)

lumbar radiculopathy · vascular claudication"] C --> F{"Trouble putting socks on?"} F -->|Yes| G["Points to HIP ARTHRITIS"] F -->|No| H["Points away from arthritis

blocks.html:
• Exam
    • look: body habitus · swelling, erythema, asymmetry or atrophy, deformity, scars (SEADS) · alignment (fixed flexion, external rotation) · gait: antalgic or Trendelenburg (weak gluteus medius and minimus → pelvis drops on the opposite side when standing on the affected leg)
    • feel: anterior superior iliac spine, anterior joint line, pubic symphysis · quadriceps, tensor fasciae latae, iliotibial band, gluteals, piriformis, hamstrings
    • move: active and passive range of motion · FABER (flexion, abduction, external rotation) · FADIR (flexion, adduction, internal rotation)
  • Investigations
    • X-ray first line (fracture, anatomical variants, arthritis, tumour, osteonecrosis)
    • ultrasound: bursitis, tendinopathy, hip dysplasia, guiding injections · CT: suspected fracture not seen on X-ray · MRI: soft tissue, stress fractures
  • Treatment (the general plan, reused below): expectations and education · protection, rest, ice, compression, elevation · weight management · exercise and physiotherapy · functional and mental support · topical or oral analgesics · corticosteroid injection · surgery
2. Anterior hip pain: inside the joint

rows: Older · primary (age-related) or secondary (trauma, FAI) · risk: female, obesity, genetics, anatomical variants
All ages, mostly young active females · FAI is the most common cause
Cartilage wears away, with reactive bone (osteophytes)
Mismatch between femoral neck and acetabulum · cam = extra bone on the femur side · pincer = extra bone on the acetabulum
Tear of the acetabular labrum, usually anterosuperior
Gradual groin pain, worse with activity and at night · morning stiffness under 30 min · crepitus · internal rotation lost first
Gradual groin pain, worse sitting, getting in and out of a car, leaning forward · "C sign"
Clicking, catching, locking · pain with exercise or lying on the side
Limited, painful internal rotation and flexion · leg-length difference · Stinchfield test
Groin pain with deep flexion and internal rotation · FABER, FADIR
X-ray: AP pelvis + frog-leg lateral · joint-space loss, osteophytes, subchondral cysts and sclerosis · graded by Kellgren-Lawrence · X-ray changes do not always match symptoms
X-ray AP and lateral (bony overgrowth) · CT for detailed shape and surgical planning
MR arthrogram (the medwiki note calls it diagnostic; the upper-year notes say it misses about 30% - check the slides)
General plan · cane in the opposite hand · acetaminophen or NSAIDs · injections · hip arthroplasty (total, hemi, resurfacing)
General plan · ~3 months of physiotherapy · arthroscopic osteoplasty
General plan · arthroscopic debridement or repair

blocks.html:
• Osteonecrosis (avascular necrosis): lost blood supply to the femoral head · after hip fracture, steroids, alcohol, lupus, sickle cell disease, radiation · groin or bone pain · X-ray
  • Also on the anterior list: iliopsoas tendinopathy or iliopsoas bursitis (internal snapping) · fracture · septic arthritis
3. Lateral hip pain

• Greater trochanteric pain syndrome (GTPS) = overuse tendinopathy of gluteus medius and minimus, with or without trochanteric bursitis
    • Who: female more than male, 40-60 years, often after menopause · poor biomechanics, a recent rise in activity
    • Presents as: pain over the greater trochanter, radiating down the lateral thigh · worse lying on that side, standing long, crossing the legs · no swelling or redness · can still put socks on (unlike hip arthritis)
    • Exam: tender greater trochanter ("jump sign") · Trendelenburg gait · single leg stance test · Ober's test · FABER and FADIR painful at the trochanter
    • Investigations: clinical diagnosis · X-ray to rule out other causes · ultrasound or MRI shows bursal inflammation or a tendon tear
    • Treatment: physiotherapy - stretch the iliotibial band, strengthen the hip abductors · load management · avoid crossing the legs, pillow between the knees · NSAIDs · steroid injection to allow physiotherapy · shock-wave therapy
  • Meralgia paresthetica = the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve trapped under the inguinal ligament
    • risk: diabetes, pregnancy, obesity, tight belts or clothing, abdominal, pelvic or hip surgery
    • burning, tingling, itching over the lateral thigh · worse standing or walking, eased by sitting · no weakness (if there is, look for another diagnosis)
    • map the numb area · diagnostic local anesthetic injection · loose clothing; conservative care usually cures it

blocks.cap: The greater trochanteric bursa sits under the iliotibial band over the greater trochanter; inflamed on the right

blocks.html: 4. Posterior hip and buttock pain

• Piriformis (deep gluteal) syndrome = the sciatic nerve compressed outside the spine, by a tight, enlarged or anatomically unusual piriformis
    • Who: female more than male, over 40 · after a fall (the most common trigger), repetitive strain, long sitting
    • Presents as: one-sided buttock pain, worse with hip flexion (sitting, stairs) · burning or shooting down the back of the thigh and leg (sciatica) · numbness, tingling, distal weakness
    • Exam: tender over the piriformis and sciatic notch · leg held externally rotated · gluteal wasting · pain on flexion, adduction and internal rotation
    • Investigations: MRI to rule out the lumbar spine (and show the swollen muscle) · electromyography (EMG) for slowed conduction beyond the compression
    • Treatment: physiotherapy (stretch piriformis) · NSAIDs · ultrasound-guided injection (steroid, trigger point, botulinum toxin) · surgical release if refractory
  • Sacroiliac joint dysfunction = too much movement in the sacroiliac joint from lax ligaments (not the same as inflammatory sacroiliitis)
    • Who: athletes · ~20% of low back pain · pregnancy (relaxin) · pelvic trauma · previous lumbar fusion or iliac crest graft
    • Presents as: one-sided buttock pain, also back, groin or leg · worse bending, climbing
    • Exam: sacroiliac joint tenderness · FABER, Gaenslen's test, sacroiliac compression test · rule out the hip
    • Treatment: pelvic belt in pregnancy · physiotherapy · sacroiliac injection (diagnostic and therapeutic) · radiofrequency ablation · fusion as a last resort
  • Also: lumbar radiculopathy (disc, facet joints, stenosis) · vascular claudication (aortoiliac disease)

lectures.name: Anatomy of the Knee - PART 1
lectures.title: Anatomy of the knee, part 1
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Valgus stresses the MCL (which drags the medial meniscus with it); varus stresses the LCL (which has no meniscus attached). ACL: weaker, taut in extension, stops the tibia sliding forward. PCL: stronger, taut in flexion, stops the tibia sliding back. The fibula is not in the knee joint. Peripheral meniscal tears heal; central ones don't. Popliteus unlocks the knee.

The knee's bones barely fit together, so it is held by soft tissue: muscles (above all the quadriceps) give dynamic support, and four cardinal ligaments plus two menisci give passive support. Knowing which structure resists which movement is what lets you name the injury in the clinical lectures.
1. Osteology

• patella = a sesamoid bone inside the quadriceps tendon
  • Femoral condyles (lateral, medial) sit on the tibial condyles (together the tibial plateau)
  • Tibial tuberosity = anterior bump where the patellar ligament inserts
  • Intercondylar area / eminence of the tibia = attachment for the cruciate ligaments and menisci
  • The fibula is NOT part of the knee joint - it does not touch the femur
2. The knee joint

• Modified synovial hinge joint: flexion and extension, plus some rotation when flexed
  • 3 articulations: lateral femoral + lateral tibial condyle · medial femoral + medial tibial condyle · femur + patella
  • Largest joint in the body, with the largest capsule and synovial membrane
  • Capsule reinforcement

blocks.html: 4. The menisci

• C-shaped fibrocartilage wedges, thick at the rim and thin in the middle: deepen the joint (better fit of the round femoral condyles) and absorb shock
  • Blood supply: rich at the periphery (from the capsule), none centrally (fed by synovial fluid) → peripheral tears can heal, central ones cannot

blocks.html: 5. Locking and unlocking: the screw-home mechanism

• Locking: in the last 15-20° of extension the femur rotates medially on the tibia → all the ligaments tighten (especially MCL, LCL, ACL) → the knee is stable for "quiet standing" with little muscle work
  • Unlocking: popliteus rotates the femur laterally (~5°) to start flexion, and pulls the lateral meniscus back out of the way
    • popliteus: lateral femoral condyle + lateral meniscus → posterior tibia above the soleal line · tibial nerve (L5, S1)

lectures.name: Clinical Approach to the Knee - PART 1
lectures.title: Clinical approach to the knee, part 1
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Pop + swelling within hours = ACL (hemarthrosis); the other ligament injuries swell little, and a meniscal tear swells late. Lachman is the best ACL test. Dashboard knee = PCL. Valgus → MCL (± medial meniscus, ± ACL = unhappy triad); varus → LCL (look for PCL and fibular nerve injury). Locking or catching = meniscus. Red-zone tears are repaired, white-zone tears resected.

An acute knee injury is named from three things: the mechanism, how fast it swelled, and which test is positive. A pop with immediate swelling is the ACL; a dashboard blow is the PCL; a valgus or varus hit is a collateral; a twist on a planted foot with locking is a meniscus.
1. General approach to knee complaints

• Symptoms: pain (aching, burning, throbbing, stabbing) · inflammatory (swelling, stiffness, redness, warmth) · neurologic (tingling, shooting, numbness, heaviness)
  • Function: structural (instability, catching, giving way, locking) · pain or nerve driven (weakness, limping, trouble walking)
  • Provoking factors: weight bearing (walking, standing, running) · stairs · sitting · inactivity
  • Investigations: X-ray, ultrasound, CT, MRI, bone scan

• Meniscal tear: degenerative ("wear and tear") or rotation / twisting with the foot planted
  • Presents as: medial or lateral joint-line pain · swelling that is delayed (1-2 days) or comes and goes · mechanical symptoms - locking, catching · giving way
  • Exam: effusion · joint-line tenderness · McMurray's test · Thessaly's test · Apley
  • Imaging: X-ray usually normal (look for knee osteoarthritis if degenerative) · MRI if conservative care fails or a large tear is suspected
  • Treatment depends on where the tear is, because only the rim has a blood supply

• Unhappy triad = MCL + medial meniscus + ACL, from a lateral (valgus) blow to a flexed knee with rotation

  • Presents as: pain, swelling, instability with twisting, locking, reduced movement, valgus laxity

lectures.name: Anatomy of the Knee - PART 2
lectures.title: Anatomy of the knee, part 2
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ The Q-angle makes the quadriceps pull the patella laterally; vastus medialis and the raised lateral femoral groove hold it in. Wider Q-angle in females → more lateral subluxation and patellofemoral pain. Genu valgum raises the Q-angle and loads the lateral condyles; genu varum lowers it and loads the medial. Housemaid's knee = prepatellar; clergyman's knee = superficial infrapatellar.

blocks.html: Built from upper-year notes and the medwiki note. Not yet checked against this year's lecture slides.

The patella always wants to slide laterally, and the knee spends structures stopping it. The angle of the femur (the Q-angle) pulls it out; the vastus medialis and a lateral ridge of bone hold it in. Around it sit the bursae that become knee bursitis.
1. The extensor mechanism and patellar stability

• Quadriceps femoris → quadriceps tendon → patella → patellar ligament → tibial tuberosity
    • the patella sits inside this tendon (a sesamoid bone), so the quadriceps are its main stabiliser
  • The pull is not straight: the femur runs diagonally, so the quadriceps pull along the femur's axis, superolaterally, while the patellar ligament pulls straight down
    • the result is a lateral force on the patella that tends to sublux it laterally
  • Two things resist the lateral pull
    • ① vastus medialis pulls the patella medially
    • ② the lateral side of the femur's patellar groove (and the larger lateral patellar facet) stands proud, a bony buttress
    • abnormal bony shape of the patella or distal femur predisposes to patellar dislocation

blocks.alt: patellar forces and lateral pull from the Q-angle - upper-year notes.jpg
blocks.cap: Quadriceps (Q) and patellar tendon (P) pulls add up to a lateral resultant (R); vastus medialis pulls back medially

blocks.html: 2. The Q-angle and knee alignment

• Q-angle = angle between a line from the anterior superior iliac spine to the patella and a line from the patella to the tibial tuberosity
  • Wider in females (wider hips) → more lateral pull → more lateral patellar subluxation and patellofemoral pain syndrome
  • Strong quadriceps with an unopposed lateral pull → the lateral patella grinds on the femur → patellofemoral pain

  • Arteries: the genicular anastomosis - superior and inferior, medial and lateral genicular branches of the popliteal artery · collateral flow from the descending branch of the lateral circumflex femoral artery

lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Anterior knee pain on stairs and after sitting, with no swelling, in a young woman = patellofemoral pain syndrome; treat by strengthening vastus medialis. Lateral knee pain while running downhill + Ober's test = iliotibial band. A popliteal cyst means something is making extra fluid - treat the cause, and don't miss a DVT. Steroid: fast, cheap, short. Hyaluronic acid: slow to wear off, expensive.

lectures.name: Anatomy of the Leg
lectures.title: Anatomy of the leg
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Anterior = dorsiflexion = deep fibular; lateral = eversion = superficial fibular; both posterior = plantarflexion = tibial. Common fibular nerve injury at the fibula → foot drop with numbness of the dorsum of the foot; deep fibular alone → numb first web space only. Tibialis anterior and tibialis posterior both invert. Tarsal tunnel: Tom, Dick And Very Nervous Harry. Gastrocnemius plantarflexes only well with the knee straight.

blocks.html: Built from upper-year notes and the medwiki note. Not yet checked against this year's lecture slides.

The leg is four sealed compartments, each with one job and one nerve: anterior dorsiflexes (deep fibular), lateral everts (superficial fibular), and both posterior compartments plantarflex (tibial). Learn that grid and nerve injuries, compartment syndrome and foot drop follow from it.
1. Bones of the leg and foot

• tibia: the weight-bearing bone · shaft just under the skin (the "shin") · tibial plateau, tuberosity, soleal line (soleus origin) · medial malleolus distally
  • fibula: posterolateral · does not bear weight (so it is the bone of choice for grafts) · head near the knee · lateral malleolus distally, longer than the medial, which limits eversion
  • Fractures: tibia at its narrowest point, between the middle and distal thirds (also its poorest blood supply) · a broken tibia often takes the fibula with it (joined by the interosseous membrane) · lateral malleolus fracture (sources differ: the medwiki note says from forced eversion; the upper-year notes say the fibula breaks just above the lateral malleolus in extreme inversion - check the slides)
  • Foot: 7 tarsals, 5 metatarsals, phalanges

rows: Gripped between the two malleoli · carries weight from the tibia to the calcaneus and forefoot · no muscle attachments
Heel, largest foot bone · calcaneal tuberosity takes the Achilles (calcaneal) tendon · sustentaculum tali: shelf for the talus and pulley for flexor hallucis longus
Between talus and the cuneiforms · its tuberosity anchors the "spring" ligament (medial arch)
Tuberosity = insertion of fibularis brevis → avulsion fracture with sudden inversion

blocks.html: 2. Fascia and compartments

• Crural fascia wraps the leg · the tibia, fibula, interosseous membrane and the anterior, posterior and transverse intermuscular septa divide it into 4 compartments
  • Retinacula stop the tendons bowstringing at the ankle: superior and inferior extensor retinacula (anterior compartment) · superior and inferior fibular retinacula (lateral compartment) · flexor retinaculum roofs the tarsal tunnel (deep posterior)
  • Compartment syndrome: the fascia does not stretch, so swelling, bleeding or infection raises the pressure → nerves and arteries in that compartment are squeezed · relieved by fasciotomy · shin splints = a mild form in the anterior compartment (overuse microtrauma where tibialis anterior attaches)

4. Tarsal tunnel

• Under the flexor retinaculum, behind the medial malleolus · front to back: "Tom, Dick And Very Nervous Harry" = Tibialis posterior · flexor Digitorum longus · posterior tibial Artery · posterior tibial Vein · tibial Nerve · flexor Hallucis longus (the upper-year notes drop the vein: "Tom, Dick And Not Harry")

  • Tarsal tunnel syndrome: tibial nerve compressed by swollen tendon sheaths → heel pain

blocks.html: 6. Veins and venous return

• Superficial (no paired artery): great saphenous vein - from the dorsal venous arch, in front of the medial malleolus, up the medial leg and thigh → femoral vein at the saphenous opening · small saphenous - from the dorsal venous arch, lateral to the Achilles tendon, up the back of the calf between the gastrocnemius heads → popliteal vein
  • Deep (paired with arteries, often 2-3 per artery): anterior and posterior tibial veins → popliteal → femoral vein
  • Perforating veins carry blood superficial → deep only (valves)
  • Return against gravity: venous valves · arteriovenous pump (pulsing artery squeezes its companion veins) · musculovenous pump (contracting muscle squeezes veins inside the tight fascia)
  • Varicose veins: valves fail, usually in the great saphenous system → blood pools distally · treated by laser closure
